An Action can override all of this. See [Actions](/kepler/actions) for how an Action pins a provider, account, model, mode, and options together, and which choice wins when they disagree.

***

## Custom agents

If your agent is not one of the 9 supported agents, you can add it by its command. To add one, open **Settings → Agents → Custom agents**, click **New custom agent**, and fill in these fields:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Name** | What the agent is called in Kepler's pickers |
| **Runs in** | **Chat** (Kepler's chat, for a program that speaks ACP) or **Terminal** (the command's own app, in a terminal) |
| **Command** | The binary to run: an absolute path, or a name Kepler resolves on your `PATH` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments for the command. For a Chat agent, the arguments that put it into ACP mode, for example `--acp` |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Variables merged into the agent's environment on every session |

Kepler treats environment values as secrets: it encrypts them at rest and hides them after you save. When you edit a custom agent, leaving a value empty (`KEY=`) keeps the stored secret, and typing a new value replaces it.

Custom agents appear alongside the built-in agents everywhere you can choose an agent. A custom agent that runs in **Terminal** works the same way as a built-in one.

***

## MCP servers

Kepler lists the MCP servers each agent loads, and lets you add, remove, sign in to, and turn off servers or single tools, per repository from the composer's **Agent settings** pill or as defaults in **Settings → Agents → MCP servers**. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

***

## Sessions

After you connect an agent, you run it in a **session** inside a task. To learn how to start and resume sessions, queue prompts, and review what the agent produced, see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

A task holds resources and does not require a worktree, or even a repository. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

To follow conversations you started outside Kepler, see [Sessions started outside Kepler](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

---

---
# MCP Servers
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/mcp-servers/
product: Kepler
feature: MCP Servers
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Your coding agents load **Model Context Protocol** (**MCP**) servers from their own config files. Kepler reads those files and lists exactly the servers each agent loads. From Kepler, without editing the agent's config by hand, you can:

- See the servers each agent loads.
- Turn a server, or one of its tools, off where you do not want it.
- Add or remove a server.
- Sign in to a server that needs it.

You manage MCP servers in 3 places:

- Per repository, from the composer's **Agent settings** pill
- Per repository, in **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers**
- As global defaults, in **Settings → Agents → MCP servers**

**Requirements and limits**

- Works for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Cursor**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, and **Grok Build**. Pi, Antigravity, and custom agents do not expose their MCP servers to Kepler. For these agents, the manager reads *This agent does not expose its MCP servers to Kepler.*
- The agent must be installed. Settings lists only the agents that answer.
- Kepler shows the servers the agent's config files define. Kepler does not list servers that are not stored on disk, such as claude.ai connectors.

***

## Where you manage them

| Where | What a change applies to |
|---|---|
| The composer's **Agent settings** pill → **MCP servers** → **Manage** | This repository, for that agent |
| **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers** | This repository, for the agent you pick |
| **Settings → Agents → MCP servers** | Every repository, as the default each one inherits |

The **MCP servers** dialog in the composer includes **Open repo settings**, which opens the same list in **Settings → Repositories**.

Every place shows the same manager. It groups servers by where they are defined:

| Group | Where the server comes from |
|---|---|
| **Added by you** | Your own config for the agent, used in every repository |
| **In this repo, shared with your team** | Checked into this repository |
| **In this repo, just you** | This repository only, not shared |
| **From plugins** | Installed by a plugin |
| **Set by your organization** | Managed by your organization |

Each row is a server. The switch on a row turns the server on or off, and clicking the row opens the server's own page. A row can carry these badges:

- **Sign in needed**: the server needs authentication before the agent can use it.
- **Every repo**: a change to the server reaches every repository.
- **Locked**: *Kepler cannot edit this entry in the agent's config file*, such as a server your organization manages.

***

## Per repository

To manage the servers for one repository:

1. In a session or in the **New task** composer, open the **Agent settings** pill. Its **MCP servers** row reads *{enabled} of {total} enabled*.
2. Click **Manage**. The **MCP servers** dialog opens. Its subtitle reads *{agent} in {repo}*, the agent and the repository the dialog applies to.

When you open a server's page, **All servers** takes you back to the list.

A change here applies to that repository and all of its worktrees.

If a server is off in Settings and you have not turned it on here, the server says *Off for every repo in Settings. Turn it on to use it here.*, with **Open Settings** to go to the global default. Turning it on in the dialog turns it on for this repository only.

### Turn off a single tool

A server's page lists its **Tools** under the **Let {agent} use this server** switch. The list can take a moment to load (*Asking the server for its tools…*). If the server needs authentication first, the list reads *Sign in to this server to see its tools.*

To turn off one tool, open the server's page and turn off the tool's switch. *Turn a tool off to keep {agent} from calling it.*

Turning off a single tool works for Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build. For the other agents, turn the whole server off instead.

***

## Global defaults

**Settings → Agents → MCP servers** is the same manager with no repository. Its description reads *Give your agents extra tools, like a database, a browser or your issue tracker.* Use the **Agent** picker at the top to choose the agent, and the account when that agent has more than one.

**Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent** is on by default. *Gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn off to manage it yourself.*

The repository and global levels combine like this:

- A repository uses the global value until you change that server in its own dialog.
- A repository's choice wins over the global one, in either direction: a repository can turn off a server that's on globally, or turn on a server that's off globally.
- Switching a server back to match the global default makes it follow the default again.

You cannot change plugin servers or Cursor servers in Settings, although plugin servers are listed there. Cursor keeps its on and off state per project, so switch a Cursor server from a repository's dialog instead.

***

## Add and remove servers

To add a server, click **Add server**: beside the section's heading in Settings, or at the foot of the list in the MCP servers dialog. The **Add MCP server ({agent})** page opens with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, or `-`, up to 64 characters, unique where it is saved |
| **Applies to** | **Every repo**, **This repo only**, or **This repo, shared with your team**. The choices depend on the agent and on whether you are in a repository, and the field shows only when there is more than 1 choice, as in a repository's **MCP servers** section |
| **Runs as** | **Command** for a local server, or **URL** or **URL (SSE)** for a remote one |
| **Command** and **Arguments** | For a command server, for example `npx -y @some/server` |
| **URL** | For a remote server, an `http://` or `https://` address |
| **Environment variables** / **Headers** | Key and value pairs. Values stay hidden until you choose **Show value** |

Kepler writes the new server into the agent's own config file, in the format that agent uses, so the agent's CLI sees it too.

To remove a server, open the server's page and click **Remove server**. Kepler deletes the server from the agent's config. You cannot undo this.

You cannot remove these servers from Kepler:

- Plugin servers.
- Managed servers.
- GitHub Copilot servers defined in a repository. You can remove only the Copilot servers in your own config.

***

## Copy a server to other agents

To use a server you already set up with another agent or account, copy it instead of adding it again. Kepler copies the server's full definition, including its environment variables and headers.

1. Open the server's page.
2. Click **Also add to…**.
3. Select each agent, or each account of an agent, that should get the server.
4. Click **Add to *N* destinations**.

Kepler adds the server to each destination in turn. If one copy fails, the others still go ahead, and the failed destination stays selected with its error.

You cannot copy servers from plugins, so their page does not show **Also add to…**.

***

## Sign in to a server

For a server that needs authentication, its page has a **Sign-in** section. It offers **Sign in**, or **Re-authenticate** once you are signed in, and **Clear authentication** to sign the server out. Kepler signs in under the same account the session uses. Credentials are saved where the agent itself looks for them. Sign-in is available for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor servers.

In a local window, **Open sign-in page** opens your browser, and Kepler finishes when you are done (*Finish signing in in your browser*). In a window connected to a remote environment, sign in on that page, then paste the URL you land on into **Redirect URL**.

If your organization manages the agent's settings, sign-in first lists them for your approval. Click **Approve and continue** to sign in, or **Decline** if you do not recognize them. Kepler saves your approval for this account.

***

## When changes apply

| Where the change lands | When it takes effect |
|---|---|
| A Claude Code **Chat** session | Straight away. Kepler reconnects the session with the new servers and keeps the conversation and your model and mode picks |
| A terminal session, or any other agent's session | On restart. The **Agent settings** pill and the dialog show *{count} MCP changes apply when the agent restarts.* with **Restart agent** |
| The **New task** composer | The session you start comes up with that state |

Where Kepler saves an on or off choice depends on the agent:

- **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot**: Kepler does not edit the agent's config, so the same agent run from your own terminal is not affected. The one exception is turning on a Claude Code server that Claude's own config lists as disabled: Kepler can do this only by editing that list.
- **Cursor and Grok Build**: Kepler writes the change into the agent's own files, which their CLIs also read.
- **Auggie**: Kepler lists the servers without a switch, because Auggie has no way to turn a server off. To stop using a server, edit Auggie's config.

Adding and removing a server always edits the config file.

Each agent account keeps its own MCP setup. Other Claude Code accounts start with the default account's servers.

***

## Related

- [Agent Settings](/kepler/settings-agents#mcp-servers): **Settings → Agents**, including the **MCP servers** section.
- [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations): the agents Kepler runs and how to set them up.
- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions): the composer's **Agent settings** pill, and restarting a session.

---

---
# Issue Tracker Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Issue Tracker Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Connect an issue tracker to see the issues you are working on in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface), alongside your pull requests and the tasks you already have running. To start work on an issue, you pick its row instead of describing the work from scratch.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

***

## Trackers Kepler can read issues from

Of Kepler's 13 providers, 11 return issues:

| Provider | Also returns pull requests |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Jira** | No |
| **Jira Server / Data Center** | No |
| **Linear** | No |
| **Trello** | No |
| **Asana** | No |

Jira, Linear, Trello, and Asana do not appear in pull-request filters.

The other 2 providers, **Bitbucket** and **Bitbucket Data Center**, return pull requests only. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** read issues the same way their cloud counterparts do. Which fields come back depends on your server's version, and your machine needs to be able to reach the server. You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted tracker](#connect-a-self-hosted-tracker).

Kepler trusts the certificates installed in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority, or a network that re-signs HTTPS traffic, works without extra setup.

***

## Connect a tracker

To connect a cloud tracker (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Azure DevOps**, **Jira**, **Linear**, **Trello**, or **Asana**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler on GitKraken's website, which opens in your browser.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account. Kepler prompts you if you are not signed in.

If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog Kepler shows while you authorize, and open it in a browser yourself. Each link works once, so **Try again** makes a new one. The dialog closes by itself once the connection appears.

### Connect a self-hosted tracker

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect *provider*** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the issues you need.
5. Click **Save connection**.

Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine, saves it on this device, and adds the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports one of these results:

- The server accepted the token.
- Kepler saved the token without being able to reach the server or verify its certificate.
- The server refused the token: *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.*

For every message the dialog shows, see [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**.

Once connected, a self-hosted provider lists each server on its own row, with **Set as primary**, **Replace token**, and **Disconnect**. Each server keeps its own repositories and issues:

- To connect another server, click **Add connection** on the provider's row. Connecting more than 1 server needs an active GitKraken plan or trial.
- To renew an expired or rejected token, click **Replace token** on that server's row.
- To make a server the provider's default connection, click **Set as primary**. Agents' GitKraken MCP server acts through the primary connection.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider's primary connection. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can also show a warning:

| Warning | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Sign-in expired** | The provider's sign-in has expired | Wait for Kepler to refresh it, or click **Reconnect** |
| **Cannot connect to server** | Kepler could not reach the server; the integration is still connected | Check that the server is reachable from your network or VPN; the warning clears on its own |
| **Unexpected response** | Kepler could not read the provider's answer, so some items may be missing | Reconnecting does not help; if it stays, check for a proxy or gateway between Kepler and the provider |
| An organization named under the row | That organization refuses Kepler's access, so only its items are left out | Follow the row's advice, such as **Request access on GitHub** |

You do not have to open Settings to find a failing provider. Todo, the **Resources** screen's lists, and a link preview name it too, with the one fix that applies: **Reconnect**, **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, **Open settings**, or **Retry**. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#where-your-pull-requests-turn-up) for each warning.

***

## Choose what Kepler brings in

Each connected integration except Trello and Asana has a visibility line under its row in **Settings → Integrations**. The line reads **Everything visible**, or how many items you have hidden.

To hide part of an integration:

1. Click **Choose what's visible…** on the provider's row. The **Choose what *provider* brings in** dialog opens.
2. Clear the checkbox of each item to hide. Type in **Filter…** to narrow a long list.
3. Click **Save**.

What the dialog lists depends on the provider:

| Provider | Lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | **Organizations** and **Repositories** |
| **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | **Organizations**, **Repositories**, and **Projects** |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear** | **Projects** |

A ticked item is visible. Hiding an organization also hides its repositories, which show *Hidden with its organization* and cannot be ticked on their own. A hidden project leaves the issue lists but stays in the project pickers. A project that has not returned any issues yet may be missing from the dialog's list.

Hidden items are left out of Todo, the issue and pull request lists, and the pickers. Tasks and branches already linked to a hidden item keep working. Kepler saves the choice on your GitKraken account, so it follows you to other machines where you sign in.

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider: two GitHub accounts, a work Jira site and a personal one. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's issues and pull requests from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary as it is. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

**Agents keep acting as the primary account.** Your agents' GitKraken MCP server always uses the primary connection of your GitKraken account, even when Kepler reads a provider through another account.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters.

**Reconnect keeps your choices.** When one account's sign-in fails, **Reconnect** renews that account's connection and keeps your primary and read choices.

The read account also authenticates Git. When you start work on an issue in a repository you have never cloned, Kepler clones that repository with the same connection it reads through. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations) for which hosts this covers and what happens on the hosts it does not.

**Linear connections stay separate by workspace.** Each Linear account's entry shows the Linear workspace it was granted. Connections to different workspaces are separate accounts, each reading only its own workspace's issues.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely, with its saved filters and its rows in your lists.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## What Kepler reads from an issue

When an issue becomes a task, Kepler attaches what it read, so the agent starts with that context instead of asking for it. Kepler reads these fields from the issue:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Identifier** | The issue key or number: `GK-1234` for Jira, `DRE-2` for Linear, a number for GitHub, GitLab, and Azure DevOps |
| **Title** | |
| **Description** | The issue body, or an Azure DevOps field such as **Repro Steps** on a Bug, labeled with its name |
| **Issue type** | The provider's own type, such as a Jira issue type |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one |
| **Assignees** | |
| **Status** | The issue's current state, in the provider's own words, such as Jira's *To Verify* |
| **Last updated** | When the issue was last updated |
| **Labels** | The provider's own labels, shown as badges in issue previews |
| **Project or board** | Jira projects, Linear teams, Azure DevOps areas. Git hosts attach issues to a repository instead |
| **Iteration or sprint** | Azure DevOps iterations and Jira sprints. A Jira issue carried across sprints keeps them all |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host, for the git hosts |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Jira**, and so on |

Kepler does not read an issue's priority field, due date, Trello checklist, or Linear cycle. An agent can still find these by opening the issue's URL itself, but Kepler does not deliver them as attached context.

Kepler reads an issue's milestone on GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab Self-Hosted, and Linear, so Todo can group and filter by **Milestone**. The agent does not receive the milestone. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

Todo's **Priority** grouping and filter come from labels instead: a label such as `P1`, `priority: high`, `blocker`, or `critical` sets the level, and the most urgent label wins. Jira and Linear keep priority in a field Kepler does not read, so their issues show as **Unprioritised** unless a label sets a priority. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

Jira and Azure DevOps descriptions keep their headings, code blocks, and tables in Kepler's previews and in the agent's context.

Images embedded in an issue's description, including Jira and Azure DevOps attachments, display in Kepler's issue previews, from self-hosted servers too. The agent receives the description as text: Kepler does not pass the attachments or images themselves.

### Comments

When you open an issue in a reader, either the task panel's side pane or the issue's pane on the task page, a **Comments** section under the summary shows its discussion. Kepler reads comments for **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Jira**, and **Jira Server / Data Center**. For other providers, the section says that comments for that provider are not available in Kepler yet.

Kepler shows up to the newest 100 comments, newest at the bottom. **Show earlier comments** shows older ones, and **Refresh comments** reads the discussion again. Comments are for you to read: Kepler does not attach them to the task or pass them to the agent.

### Which issues Kepler lists

Kepler lists open work. An issue that is finished or canceled in its tracker (a Linear issue in *Done* or *Canceled*, for example) leaves **Todo** and the issue pickers. An issue already attached to a task keeps showing on that task with its real state, finished or not.

A Todo view has 2 scopes, set in its **View** menu under **Scope**:

- **Mine**: the issues related to you, across every organization you belong to.
- **All**: also adds the open issues of the repositories added to Kepler on GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, and GitLab Self-Hosted. On other providers, it lists the same issues as **Mine**.

Under **All**, **Repos** and **Updated** narrow the view by repository and by how recently each issue was updated. **All repos in Kepler** skips a very large repository and says so, with **Choose repos** to add it anyway.

Under **Mine**, each provider reports a different set of issues related to you:

| Provider | Issues Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or mentioning you |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Yours or assigned to you |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear**, **Trello**, **Asana** | Assigned to you |

An issue listed only because you were mentioned is marked **Mentioned**, so you can tell it apart from work that is yours. Under **All**, the **Your role** filter also offers **Not mine**.

To find issues to add to a task, the issue list on a task's **Resources** screen has its own scope menu: **Related to me**, **All in my repos** (the open issues in the repositories added to Kepler), or **All visible**.

For GitHub and Azure DevOps, **All visible** reads every issue across your organizations, including repositories you can read outside them, such as ones where you are an outside collaborator. It loads more slowly. Jira and Linear show only your issues there until you pick a project or a team:

- **Jira**: when the issue list shows Jira alone, a project picker appears, starting with **All projects**. Pick a project to see every open issue in it. Kepler remembers the pick for each Jira connection.
- **Linear**: when the issue list shows Linear alone, a team picker and a **Project** picker appear. Pick a team, a Linear project, or both, to see every open issue in them, whoever it is assigned to. The **Project** picker lists your Linear workspace's projects with their state, closed ones included. Changing the team clears the project pick.

**A Linear issue synced with GitHub shows once.** When Linear's GitHub Issues sync keeps a two-way copy of a Linear issue on GitHub, Kepler lists the pair as one row, the Linear issue. The pair shares one task history, so a task started from either copy is the issue's task. Pairing works for GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

When you start work from the Linear issue, Kepler uses the repository of its GitHub copy if exactly one repository you have in Kepler matches it.

***

## Where your issues turn up

Your issues appear in 3 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | A **Todo** view lists your issues across every connected tracker, grouped and filtered how you like |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button on a row hands the issue to an agent with its context attached. Running an Action on an issue that has no task also turns it into a task |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | An issue is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

The **Issue type**, **Label**, **Project**, and **Status** filters use your provider's own terms, not Kepler's. Azure DevOps and Jira issues also filter by **Iteration** and **Sprint**, each named the way its tracker names it.

Kepler recognizes an issue from its URL when you paste or attach one, including these work item URLs:

- **GitLab** work items, at `/-/work_items/<number>` in a project. A group-level work item stays a plain link.
- **Azure DevOps** work items, at `/<organization>/<project>/_workitems/edit/<number>` or at the organization level, `/<organization>/_workitems/edit/<number>`.

**Search by key or link.** In the issue list of a task's **Resources** screen, type a Jira or Linear issue key, such as `OPS-42`, or paste a Jira Cloud, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, or Azure DevOps work item link. Kepler finds that issue in its tracker, whatever its state, even when it is not in the list. A Jira Server / Data Center link resolves when it points at an installation you have connected.

**Jira keys in commits and branches.** With Jira or Jira Server / Data Center connected, Kepler links Jira issue keys in commit messages and branch names, so `OPS-42` in a commit message links to that issue. Right-click a commit in a worktree's commit list for **Open issue *key*** and **Copy issue URL for *key*** (see [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes#the-changes-panel)), and the **Worktrees and branches** page shows the keys as chips on branch and worktree rows (see [Repository Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#worktrees-and-branches)). Only Jira keys are linked this way.

**Add from the list with the keyboard.** In the issue list on the **Resources** screen, the arrows move between rows, and **Enter** or a double-click adds the row. **Show preview** in the screen's header shows the picked row beside the list. See [Picking issues and pull requests](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#picking-issues-and-pull-requests).

**Paste a link on the Links tab.** An issue URL pasted on the **Links** tab of the **Resources** screen is looked up and added as that issue, with **Add as plain link** to keep it a plain link. See [Pasting an issue link](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#pasting-an-issue-link).

**Paste a link into a prompt.** Paste an issue or pull request URL into a session's or a new task's composer and it becomes a link chip, which Kepler attaches to the task when you send. See [Sending a prompt](/kepler/agent-sessions#sending-a-prompt).

---

---
# Pull Request Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/pull-request-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Pull Request Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Connect a Git host to see the pull requests you authored, and the ones waiting on your review, in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). Kepler also matches each pull request to your existing worktrees, so a branch you are working on shows its pull request wherever the branch appears.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

Each connected Git host has a visibility line under its row. The line reads **Everything visible**, or shows how many items you have hidden. To leave organizations or repositories out of Todo, the lists, and the pickers, click **Choose what's visible…**. See [Choose what Kepler brings in](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#choose-what-kepler-brings-in).

***

## Hosts Kepler can read pull requests from

Of Kepler's 13 providers, 8 return pull requests:

| Provider | Also returns issues |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Bitbucket** | No |
| **Bitbucket Data Center** | No |

Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center do not appear in issue filters.

The other 5 providers (Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, Trello, and Asana) return issues only. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** read pull requests and merge requests the same way their cloud counterparts do. Which fields come back depends on your server's version.

You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted instance](#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). Your machine needs to be able to reach the server. Kepler trusts the certificates in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority works without extra setup.

Kepler shows GitLab merge requests as pull requests, in the same list.

***

## Connect a Git host

To connect a cloud Git host (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Bitbucket**, or **Azure DevOps**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler on GitKraken's website, which opens in your browser.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account.

If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog Kepler shows while you authorize, and open it in a browser yourself. Each link works once, so **Try again** makes a new one. The dialog closes by itself once the connection appears. **Reconnect** uses the same dialog.

### Connect a self-hosted instance

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect *provider*** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the repositories you need.
5. Click **Save connection**.

The address must be `http` or `https`, without credentials, a query, or a fragment. Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine, saves it on this device, and adds the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports how the check went:

| Message | What it means |
|---|---|
| *Credentials verified with the server.* | The server accepted the token |
| *Credentials saved. Unable to verify the server certificate. Check its TLS configuration.* | Kepler saved the token but could not verify the server's certificate |
| *Credentials saved without verification. Unable to reach the server.* | Kepler saved the token without checking it |
| *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.* | Fix the token and save again |

Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**, and you cannot make that connection the primary. If Kepler cannot reach GitKraken, it retries when you refresh your providers.

Once connected, a self-hosted provider lists each server on its own row, with **Set as primary**, **Replace token**, and **Disconnect**. Each server keeps its own repositories and pull requests:

- To connect another server, click **Add connection** on the provider's row. Connecting more than 1 server needs an active GitKraken plan or trial.
- To renew an expired or rejected token, click **Replace token** on that server's row. If you change the server's address there, Kepler disconnects the previous server before it adds the new one.
- To make a server the provider's default connection, click **Set as primary**.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can show a warning:

- **Sign-in expired**: the token needs refreshing. Kepler tries to refresh it by itself; **Reconnect** refreshes it by hand.
- **Cannot connect to server**: the integration is still connected, but Kepler could not reach the server. Instead of reconnecting, check that the server is up and reachable from your network or VPN.
- An organization named under the row: that organization refuses Kepler's access, such as a GitHub organization that restricts OAuth apps. Kepler leaves out only that organization's items.

See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) for the warnings in full.

***

## Cloning a repository for a pull request

When you start work on a pull request from a repository you have never cloned, Kepler first clones the repository into your **Repositories folder** (**Settings → Repositories**). On GitHub and GitLab, the clone signs in through your connected account, so a private repository clones without a Git credential helper. How the clone authenticates depends on the host:

| Host | How the clone authenticates |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Your connected account's token |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Your connected account's token |
| **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Your own Git credentials |

A self-hosted repository clones through the account connected to that server. When a provider has more than one account, the clone uses the account Kepler reads from: **Read from this account** where you set one, otherwise the primary.

Kepler does not write the token into the clone's `.git/config` or the remote's URL.

If Kepler has no usable token for the host, the clone uses your own Git credential helper. Kepler cannot prompt you for Git credentials, so with no credential helper the clone fails. To fix it, sign in with a Git credential helper (for example, `gh auth login`) or use an SSH URL, then try again.

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's pull requests and issues from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary alone. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

**Agents keep acting as the primary account.** Your agents' GitKraken MCP server always uses the primary connection of your GitKraken account, even when Kepler reads a provider through another account.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely, with its saved filters and its rows in your lists.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## How pull requests attach to worktrees

Kepler matches a pull request to a worktree by its branch, so a branch shows its pull request, even after the pull request merges.

### Auto-attaching a matched pull request

When you open a pull request outside Kepler (with `gh` in a terminal, from GitKraken Desktop, or on the web), Kepler attaches it to the task for you. The pull request then behaves like one you attached yourself: it appears in the task's resources, and the agent receives it as context. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

Kepler auto-attaches a pull request only when all of these are true:

- It is open.
- Its head branch exactly matches a worktree's branch on an active task, in the same repository (not from a fork).
- It is yours: you opened it, or your branch pushes to it. A teammate's pull request on a branch with the same name is not attached; attach it yourself if you need it.

Kepler never removes or replaces a link. Several active tasks can share one pull request.

***

## What Kepler reads from a pull request

Kepler reads these fields from a pull request:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Number and title** | |
| **Description** | The pull request body |
| **State** | **Open**, **Draft**, **Merged**, or **Closed** |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one. A row shows **Yours** for a pull request you authored, and **Review** for someone else's |
| **Head and base branch** | When the provider reports them |
| **Fork** | Whether the head branch lives on a fork, and where |
| **Created at** | |
| **Checks and review** | Shown on an open or draft pull request's chip in a task panel: failing, pending, or passing checks, and an approved review |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Bitbucket**, and so on |

A merged pull request keeps its description and author for as long as a task, archived or not, still links it.

Images embedded in a pull request's description display in Kepler's previews, including on GitHub Enterprise, GitLab Self-Hosted, and Azure DevOps Server. On Bitbucket Data Center, an embedded image may show as a link instead.

***

## Where your pull requests turn up

Your pull requests appear in 4 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | A **Todo** view lists the pull requests related to you on each connected host, or every open one in the repositories added to Kepler |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button hands the pull request to an agent. **Review** and **Address Feedback** are the 2 built-in Actions for pull requests, and Kepler picks one based on who authored the pull request |
| [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes) | Reading the diff and the commits behind a pull request |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | A pull request is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

**Todo's scope.** A Todo view's **View** menu sets its **Scope**: **Mine**, the work related to you, or **All**, which adds the open pull requests of the repositories added to Kepler on every Git host above. See [Which issues Kepler lists](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#which-issues-kepler-lists).

Under **Mine**, each provider reports a different set of pull requests related to you, so Todo lists these from each:

| Host | Pull requests Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or ones you review |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | Yours or awaiting your review |
| **Bitbucket** | Yours, or awaiting your review in your workspaces and repositories added to Kepler |

The pull request list on a task's **Resources** screen has its own scope menu: **Related to me** or **All in my repos**.

**Review requests come from every host.** Pull requests waiting on your review show up from every Git host above. On a large Bitbucket workspace, review requests can take a while to appear.

**Lists stay current while you look at them.** Pull request and issue lists refresh while they are on screen, and again when you come back to the window. When one provider fails to load, the others keep loading, and the failed provider's last loaded pull requests stay in the list.

**A failing provider is named, with its fix.** When a connected provider's read fails, Todo, the **Resources** screen's lists, and a link preview show a warning that names the provider and the fix, such as *Sign in to GitHub again to load its work.* Each warning offers one fix:

| What went wrong | The fix offered |
|---|---|
| The sign-in needs renewing | **Reconnect**, or **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, which needs a new token |
| The provider refused part of the request, so some organizations or repositories are missing | **Open settings** |
| Rate limiting, an unreachable server, an unreadable answer, or a temporary problem | **Retry** |

On Todo, each warning also has **Filter out *provider***, which hides that provider from the Todo view so it stops reporting the failure. To show the provider again, clear it in the view's **Provider** filter.

Rows kept from the last good load show a cloud mark on their provider chip.

**The pull request picker says why its list is empty.** When you add a pull request from the **Resources** screen, the picker explains an empty list:

- If the **Linked work** filter hides pull requests, the picker says how many it hides and which filter hides them, and offers **Show all**.
- If no connected provider can list pull requests, the picker reads **Connect your code host** and lists the providers that can fill the tab, each with **Connect**.

The **Linked work** filter defaults to **No active task**. A task counts as active until you archive it, so Done and on-hold tasks count. The filter has 5 options:

| Option | Shows pull requests |
|---|---|
| **Any** | Whatever their task history |
| **No active task** | With no task, or with archived tasks only |
| **No tasks ever** | Never linked to a task |
| **Has an active task** | Linked to at least one task that is not archived |
| **Archived tasks only** | Linked only to archived tasks |

A row with task history carries a badge that says how many tasks it belongs to, and whether they are archived.

When nothing you have connected can list issues or pull requests, **Add issue** and **Add PR** in the **New task** composer open on a connect view, **Connect where your work lives**. Connect each provider you use, then click **Continue**. On the **Resources** screen, an empty list offers **Connect your code host** or **Connect your issue tracker** instead.

You can also start work on a pull request from GitLens or GitKraken Desktop. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).

---

---
# Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use Settings to change how Kepler, your agents, and your tasks work. Settings has 15 pages, listed in [The Settings pages](#the-settings-pages).

To open Settings, click the gear icon in the top bar, or press **⌘ ,** (**Ctrl ,** on Windows and Linux). To close it, click the gear icon or press the same shortcut again.

***

## The Settings pages

The Settings sidebar starts with a **Search settings** field and [**Setup**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#setup), a progress ring that reopens the first-run checklist. Below them, it lists these pages:

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [**Account**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#account) | Who you're signed in as, your organization, what your plan unlocks, and GitKraken AI credits |
| [**Agents**](/kepler/settings-agents) | Your agents, custom agents, MCP servers, agent tools, approvals, and usage limits |
| [**Tasks**](/kepler/settings-tasks) | How new tasks start, including the default agent, and how a task's page looks |
| [**Repositories**](/kepler/settings-repositories) | The repositories folder, your repos and folders, worktrees and branches, and Projects |
| [**Integrations**](/kepler/settings-integrations) | Issue tracker and Git host connections, and sessions started in your own terminal |
| [**Actions**](/kepler/settings-actions) | Suggested Actions per item kind, and the Action list |
| [**General**](/kepler/settings-app#general) | Language, the chat's send key, the default editor, windows, keeping agents running, and usage insights |
| [**Notifications**](/kepler/settings-app#notifications) | Which agent events notify you, on the desktop and in Kepler |
| [**Appearance**](/kepler/settings-app#appearance) | Light or dark appearance and themes, the Dashboard's views, the chat, the terminal font, the code font, and diff layout |
| [**Voice**](/kepler/settings-app#voice) | Dictation, with its models and learned words, and read aloud, all on this device |
| [**Keyboard shortcuts**](/kepler/settings-app#keyboard-shortcuts) | Kepler's keyboard shortcuts, and the keys you choose for them |
| [**Remote environments**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-environments) | The machines your agents can run on, over SSH or WSL |
| [**Remote Access**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-access) | Opening this Kepler from another device |
| [**Updates**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#updates) | The installed version and app updates |
| [**Help**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#help) | The docs, release notes, onboarding guides, and Kepler's logs |

The account menu also opens **Account**.

### Find a setting

To find a setting by name, start typing when Settings opens: **Search settings** already has focus. Search also matches help text and common synonyms, so a word like *theme* or *notifications* finds the right section.

When a search result or an Ask Kepler link takes you to a setting, Kepler highlights its control. If the setting is not shown, for example because it depends on something you have not set up yet, Kepler says why.

Ask Kepler can also search Kepler's settings, and change one when you ask. It names the setting as a link you can click. Some changes need your approval first. Settings that hold secrets, such as your account or integrations, can only be linked. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

To jump to a section, use the section links the Settings sidebar shows under the page you have open. Under **Agents**, the sidebar also lists each supported agent below **Your agents**.

### Sub-pages and unsaved changes

When you open an item to edit it, such as a repository, a project, a custom agent, an MCP server, or an Action, it opens as a sub-page inside its Settings page, with a breadcrumb back to the page.

A sub-page form saves when you click **Save** in its footer. If a save fails, the footer shows why and keeps your edits on the form.

If you leave a sub-page with unsaved changes, however you leave, Kepler asks whether to save them before it discards anything.

Most fields outside those forms save themselves and show their status beside them. If a save fails, Kepler shows the reason, and names the setting if you have already left the page.

**Go back**, or your mouse's back button, steps back through each page, sub-page, and search result you opened in Settings. To leave Settings in one click from any page or sub-page, use the back arrow in the Settings header, the gear icon, or **⌘ ,** (**Ctrl ,**). When the Dashboard's [views](/kepler/settings-app#dashboard) sit **Along the left side**, the back arrow sits at the top of the views column instead. Each one returns you to what you were doing before you opened Settings.

### Settings in a remote window

In a window connected to a remote environment, Settings shows that machine's settings, and its header names the machine. Under its title, each page says where its settings are saved:

- **Saved on {machine}**: on the remote machine.
- **Saved on this machine**: on your own computer, for every Kepler window on it.

A section that saves somewhere other than its page has its own badge. To change this machine's own settings from a remote window, click **Open this machine's settings** in the header. The same page opens in a local window.

Some settings are kept on your own computer, such as the language, the default editor, the themes, the terminal and code fonts, and the diff layout. If Ask Kepler in a remote window changes one of these, the change applies on your computer, and a notification names it, with **Undo**. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

---

---
# Setup and Account Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-setup-account/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Setup** to get back to Kepler's first-run checklist. Use **Account** to see who you are signed in as, which organization you are acting as, what your plan includes, and how you are using your GitKraken AI credits.

## Setup

To reopen the first-run checklist, click **Setup** at the top of the Settings sidebar, under **Search settings**. Its progress ring shows how much of the checklist is done. For what the checklist asks you to do, and how to hide it from the toolbar, see [Getting Started → Finish the setup checklist](/kepler/kepler-getting-started#finish-the-setup-checklist).

***

## Account

The **Account** page has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Account** | Who you are signed in as, with your name and email |
| Organization | Your active organization and its plan. If your GitKraken account belongs to more than 1 organization, this line is a switcher |
| **Refresh account status** | Reads your plan again. Kepler also picks up a purchase or plan change you make outside the app by itself, without a restart |
| **Manage account** / **Manage subscription** | Opens your GitKraken account or subscription on gitkraken.dev |
| **Unlock more with Kepler** | What this plan includes and what it does not. Shown only while something is left to unlock |
| **GitKraken AI credits** | Your credit balance, with **Buy credits**, and **Your usage by feature**. Shown only when there is a balance to show |

The organization you are acting as decides what a feature costs and whether it is unlocked at all.

**Your usage by feature** shows where your AI credits went. It appears once you have used an AI feature. A stacked bar splits your use between your 3 most-used AI features and everything else, shown as **Other**. Below the bar, each feature has a row with its share of your use as a percentage, such as **Commit Message**, **Conflict Resolution**, **Compose Changes**, or **Task & branch names**. To see what a feature does, hover its help icon.

### When a feature is locked

If a feature is locked on the organization you are acting as but included on another organization you belong to, Kepler offers to switch instead of showing a paywall: *{organization} ({plan}) already includes this.*, with **Switch to organization**.

If you just changed your plan, use **Check again** under **Already upgraded?** on the paywall. If nothing has changed, the paywall reads *Still on {plan}*. A paywall that covers the whole window also shows an account card with **Signed in as**, your **Current organization**, and a **Switch** button for each other organization whose plan includes the feature.

### Trials

When a trial starts, a dialog reads **You just opened up all of Kepler**, with a pill that shows how many days are free (*{count} days free*). It lists what the trial unlocks: *Every feature below is yours until {date}.*

When the trial ends, a dialog reads **Your trial has ended** and lists **What your trial included**. It offers an upgrade or, if your account can start the trial again, a way to continue where you stopped.

---

---
# Agent Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-agents/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Settings → Agents** to install and update the coding agents that work on your tasks, sign in to them, choose how each one starts, and give them more tools.

At the top of the page, a line names the agent new sessions start with. To change it, click **Change in Tasks**, which opens [Default agent](/kepler/settings-tasks#default-agent).

To choose the agent Ask Kepler uses, set **New Ask Kepler chats start with**. It is separate from the default for tasks. Its agent-settings pill saves the agent, account, [agent preset](#agent-presets), model, and options as you pick them. Below it, **Start each chat on the agent you used last** is on by default: your first chat uses the pill's agent, and each later chat starts on your last pick. To always start on the pill's agent, clear it.

**New Ask Kepler chats start with** lists only the agents that run in **Chat**, because only they can answer in the Ask Kepler panel. See [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler#which-agents-can-answer).

## Your agents

Kepler supports **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Pi**, **Auggie**, **Antigravity**, **Cursor**, and **Grok Build**. Settings lists the agents installed on this machine first.

In the section header, **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater, and **Rescan** looks again for the agent CLIs installed on this machine. If you install or remove an agent outside Kepler, click **Rescan**.

Each agent has a card. The card's title line shows the agent's name and these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Version | The installed version, **Not installed**, or **Version unknown** when Kepler could not read the version |
| **Update** | Runs the agent's updater and streams its output. Shown when Kepler has an updater for that agent |
| **Install** | Opens **Set up {name}** to pick an install method, then **Sign in to {name}** if the agent needs a sign-in. Shown when the agent is not installed and has an installer for your OS |
| **Enabled** | *Off keeps it installed but hidden when you start work.* |

If you installed the agent yourself, use **Already installed?** in the same dialog: enter or browse to the program, then click **Use this**.

When the version is unknown, Kepler turns off features that depend on the version, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. To fix it, reinstall or update the agent.

If the installed version of an agent has a known problem, a warning note on the card names the version and says what to do:

| Note | What it means |
|---|---|
| *OpenCode {version} is not supported* | Sessions with this version do not start. Install OpenCode 2, or choose an OpenCode 2 binary under **Program and data folder** |
| *Auggie {version} may not load your MCP servers in chat* | With this version, Chat sessions may skip the MCP servers in Auggie's own settings, and a server whose path contains spaces or parentheses may fail to start |
| *Codex {version} can show approval prompts that need no answer* | Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

The card body holds the rest:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Accounts** | Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build: runs more than 1 login side by side. See [Use several accounts for one agent](#use-several-accounts-for-one-agent) |
| **Account** | On an agent with a single login: who is signed in, with **Sign in** or **Sign out**. Signing out deletes the stored credentials |
| **New sessions start in** | The default mode for new sessions. See below |
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Program and data folder** | A disclosure holding **Binary** and **Data folder** |

Under **Program and data folder**:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Binary** | The agent program Kepler runs. **Auto** uses the first match on your `PATH`, the same one `which` finds. To override it, pick a specific install or **Custom path…**, or click **Rescan** to search again | Auto |
| **Data folder** | *Overrides the agent's default data and config folder.* | Empty, meaning the agent's own default |

**OpenCode needs version 2.** If you have both versions installed, point **Binary** at OpenCode 2. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes in OpenCode 2.

**Google Antigravity runs the `agy` CLI in both modes.** Chat needs Antigravity CLI 1.5.0 or newer. With an older CLI, click **Update** on its card. One sign-in, **Sign in in Terminal**, serves both Chat and Terminal. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations#sign-in-to-an-agent).

### Use several accounts for one agent

With **Accounts**, you can run more than 1 login for an agent side by side. Each account has its own credentials and history, but shares your skills, agents, commands, and settings.

To add an account, click **Add account**. For Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot, also choose whether its conversations **Keep separate** or **Share with the CLI**. A new Copilot account starts on **Share with the CLI**, and its new conversations use your CLI settings. If you change a Copilot account's choice later, the conversations it already has stay where they are and still open in Kepler.

Each account row has the following controls:

- A color picker that tints the agent icon wherever that account runs. The default account starts with **No color**.
- **Sign in**.
- An account menu with **Rename**, **Share history with the CLI**, **Sign in another way**, **Sign out**, and **Remove account**. On a signed-in Claude Code account, the menu also has **Switch account…**, which signs that account in with a different Claude login. See [Switch the account a Claude Code login uses](#switch-the-account-a-claude-code-login-uses).

Removing an account stops its running sessions and deletes the sessions stored only in that account. To keep those sessions, click **Move to CLI account** first. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#several-accounts-for-one-agent).

### When an added account stops sharing your settings

An added account shares your own settings, instructions, skills, agents, commands, and other configuration. If the agent saves a change while signed in to that account, it can write its own copy, and the account stops following your file. Kepler then shows a message under the account's row. Expand it to see both files, and choose one of the following:

- **Ask Kepler to resolve** opens an Ask Kepler chat with a prompt you can edit, asking the agent to copy what is worth keeping into your shared copy.
- **Share your {item} again** links the account back to your file, and saves its own copy as a backup next to it.
- **Keep its own {item}** keeps the account's copy. You can still choose **Share your {item} again** later from the row's menu.

### Switch the account a Claude Code login uses

**Switch account…** opens a dialog that names the login now signed in, and how many running sessions use the account. Running sessions pick up the new login when they restart or on their next request. On the default account, the one the CLI uses, the switch also changes the account the `claude` command uses in your own terminals.

Click **Continue** to open the usual sign-in. If your browser is already signed in, choose a different account on the sign-in page.

### Default mode for new sessions

Every agent that can run in both Chat and Terminal has this setting:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **New sessions start in** | **Chat** runs the agent inside Kepler; **Terminal** runs the agent's own command-line app | Chat. Google Antigravity starts on Terminal |

Kepler saves the choice per agent, so one agent can default to Terminal while another stays on Chat. The setting is only a default: you can pick the other mode when you start a session. A terminal-only agent shows **Terminal** with no switch. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

### Artifacts in new sessions

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Gives new sessions the Artifact tools, which publish pages and designs and add about 12k tokens to each session's context | Off |

A running Chat session has its own **Artifacts** switch in its agent settings. When you turn it on, Kepler asks first, then restarts the session and resumes the conversation. Once a conversation has artifacts on, they stay on for that conversation. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

### Let artifact comments start turns

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Lets anyone with edit access to an artifact a Chat session publishes start a turn in that session by sending a comment to Claude | On |

Running sessions keep the value they started with. When you change the setting, the card lists the sessions still on the previous value. To apply the new value, click **Restart all**, or tick sessions and click **Restart selected**.

Restarting keeps each conversation. It interrupts a turn in progress and stops background work, and a restarted session stops watching the artifacts it published before.

## Custom agents

To run an agent that Kepler does not list, add it as a custom agent by giving Kepler its command. To add one, click **New custom agent** in the section header. To edit one, click its row. Either way, the agent opens as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name Kepler shows for the agent |
| **Command** | The program to run, for example `/usr/local/bin/my-agent` or `my-agent` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments passed to the command |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Environment for the command |
| **Runs in** | **Chat**: *Kepler's chat. Needs a program that speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol).* **Terminal**: *The command's own app, in a terminal.* |

Custom agents appear with the built-in agents wherever you pick an agent.

Kepler encrypts environment values at rest and hides existing values when you edit an agent. To keep a stored secret, leave its value empty (`KEY=`). To replace it, type a new value.

**Delete** asks first, then deletes the agent and the environment values stored with it. You cannot undo a delete.

## Agent presets

An agent preset saves one agent's model, mode, and other options, such as effort, under a name, so you can pick them all at once whenever you pick that agent. The list groups your presets by agent, with the agent's badge beside each name:

- To add a preset, click **New preset** in the section header, or click **Save preset** in a session's agent settings.
- To edit a preset, click its row.
- To duplicate, reorder, or delete a preset, use its menu.

A preset opens as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | A name no other preset uses |
| **Agent** | The agent the preset belongs to, with its **Model**, **Mode**, and other options |

You can use a preset in these places:

- **A session's agent settings.** In the composer, pick it in the **Preset** row, which appears when the chosen agent has presets. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#agent-model-mode-and-effort).
- **The default agents.** The **New sessions start with** pill on [Default agent](/kepler/settings-tasks#default-agent), and the **New Ask Kepler chats start with** pill at the top of this page.
- **Actions.** Each Action's **Preset** list, in the Action's editor. See [Actions](/kepler/actions).
- **Automations.** An automation's agent settings can use a preset. See [Automations](/kepler/automations).

If Actions or automations use a preset you delete, Kepler lists them and asks you to choose a replacement. If you change a preset that automations use, Kepler names them and asks you to confirm, and they use the updated options from their next run.

When you change a preset, running sessions that use it keep the earlier version until you update them. To apply the change, click **Update all** below the list. Updating keeps each conversation, but a session that needs a restart interrupts any turn in progress.

## MCP servers

Use **MCP servers** to give your agents extra tools, like a database, a browser, or your issue tracker. The servers here are each agent's own defaults, and every repository inherits them.

To see the servers an agent loads, pick the agent with **Agent**. If that agent has more than 1 account, pick an account too. Kepler lists only the agents that expose their MCP servers to Kepler. In the list:

- Click a server to open its own page. There you can turn the server or a single tool off, sign in to a server that needs it, use **Also add to…** to copy the server to another agent, and **Remove server**.
- Click **Add server** in the section header to add one.

A server or tool you turn off here is off in every repository, unless a repository turns it back on for itself. A repository's own **MCP servers** section is on its [Edit repo](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository) page. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

Below the list, one more setting applies across every agent:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent** | *Gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn off to manage it yourself.* | On |

Separately, every session Kepler starts gets Kepler's own workspace tools, which are always on and have no setting. They let the agent work with your tasks and their notes, links, files, and worktrees, with sessions, approvals, and [themes](/kepler/settings-app#theme), and rebase, merge, and compose commits when [Agent tools](#agent-tools) turns them on. An agent can name a repository by one of its [aliases](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository). For the full list of tools, see [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

Workspace tools run without the agent's own permission prompt, in both Chat and Terminal. Instead, an action that needs your approval, such as deleting a worktree or changing another task, waits for you on an approval card. See [Approvals](#approvals).

## Agent tools

Use **Agent tools** to let your agents call Kepler's own tools for rebasing, merging, and cleaning up commits:

| Setting | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **AI Sync** | *Lets agents rebase or merge your branch and resolve conflicts for you. Every change can be undone.* | Off |
| **AI Compose** | *Lets agents turn messy changes into clean, focused commits. Every change can be undone.* | Off |

You need a paid GitKraken subscription to turn either one on. Without one, a setting that is off shows a lock in place of its checkbox. A setting that is already on keeps its checkbox, so you can still turn it off.

A change applies to new agent sessions. Sessions already running keep the tools they started with.

## Approvals

Some actions your agents take wait for your approval. Use **Approvals** to manage the rules that approve those actions for you. An action that no rule covers still asks.

When an agent uses Kepler's workspace tools to do something that needs your approval, Kepler pins an approval card above that session's message box. Examples include deleting a worktree, sending a prompt to another session, or rewriting a branch. The card's **Approve** menu offers **Always approve** for that kind of action. Kepler does not offer it for actions that can lose work, or for a setting change that Ask Kepler asks to make. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

**Always approved** lists each rule you create this way, with when and where you added it and how often it has run. **Remove** deletes the rule, so that kind of action asks again.

## Usage limits

These settings control how Kepler handles your agent plans' usage limits:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** | Asks each agent's provider for your plan usage, per-model limits, and extra usage, with the agent's own sign-in | On |
| **Resume after the usage limit resets** | When a usage limit cuts off a turn and nothing is queued, sends a "continue" message shortly after the limit resets | Off |

Kepler uses the agent's sign-in only to ask its provider, and never changes it. With **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** off, Kepler shows only what agents report, and sends a message queued at a usage limit automatically only if the agent says when the limit resets.

***

---
